pos: n. (Philipp Jakob Spener, 1635–1705, Lutheran pastor at Frankfurt, Dresden and Berlin, father of German Pietism)
etymology: Greek Philippos, lover of horses; Spener, an Alsatian surname.
biblical_def: Philipp Jakob Spener was senior minister at Frankfurt when, in 1670, he began gathering a few earnest members in his house twice a week to read Scripture and apply the Sunday sermon — the collegia pietatis, from which the name Pietism comes. In 1675 he published Pia Desideria, a preface to a volume of Arndt's sermons that became the manifesto of the movement: more extensive use of the word among the people, revival of the priesthood of all believers, insistence that Christianity is practice and not knowledge only, controversy conducted in love and prayer rather than abuse, reform of ministerial training toward godliness, and preaching aimed at edification rather than display. The dictionary holds that the diagnosis was largely right and that the remedy, left to itself, tended to subordinate doctrine to experience. 1Pe 2:9 is the priesthood he invoked. Act 2:42 the pattern of the house meetings. Jas 1:27 the practical test he applied.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pietism as a sect of Christians who profess great strictness and purity of life; and edification, as improvement and progress of the mind in knowledge or in holiness.
webster_full: PI'ETISM, n. The principles or practice of the Pietists.
PI'ETIST, n. One of a sect professing great strictness and purity of life, despising learning, school-theology and ecclesiastical polity.
EDIFICA'TION, n. Improvement and progress of the mind, in knowledge, in morals, or in faith and holiness.
scriptures: But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
corruption_summary: Spener diagnosed a Lutheranism orthodox in every article and cold in every pew, and the cure outran the diagnosis.
corruption_paragraphs: The six proposals of Pia Desideria are, taken one by one, hard to fault. More Scripture among the people is 2Ti 3:16 applied; the priesthood of all believers is 1Pe 2:9 quoted; controversy in love is commanded repeatedly. What later Pietism did with them is another matter. Where the house meeting became the real church and the public ministry an afterthought, and where the question whether a man had experienced the new birth displaced the question whether his doctrine was true, the movement bred the subjectivism the orthodox had feared.

The dictionary names that drift as the corruption, and notes that it is the parent of much in modern evangelicalism: the small group as the locus of spiritual reality, the testimony as the test of standing, doctrine treated as the cold part of religion. Act 2:42 keeps the apostles' doctrine first in a list of four and keeps all four in the church's continuing life. Jas 1:27 keeps the test visible and moral rather than inward and unverifiable.
roots_lines: Greek genos (G1085) — a race, a generation; 1 Peter 2:9.
usage: “a chosen generation, a royal priesthood” (1Pe 2:9) — the second proposal.
“continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship” (Act 2:42) — doctrine first.
“Pure religion and undefiled before God” (Jas 1:27) — the practical test.

pos: n. (Latin, Pious Desires; Philipp Jakob Spener's reform programme of 1675, the founding document of German Pietism)
etymology: Latin pius, dutiful, devout; desiderium, a longing, a desire.
biblical_def: Pia Desideria is a short book, written first as a preface, in three parts: a description of the corrupt condition of the church in its civil rulers, its clergy and its people; an argument that a better state is to be hoped for; and six proposals to reach it. The six are the famous part. Bring the word of God more richly among the people, by private reading and household and group study as well as public preaching. Establish and exercise the spiritual priesthood of all believers. Press that Christianity consists in practice and not in knowledge alone. Conduct religious controversies with prayer, example and love rather than contempt. Reform the universities so that ministers are formed in godliness as well as learning. Preach to edify the inner man rather than to display rhetoric. 2Ti 3:16 and Act 17:11 stand behind the first; 1Pe 2:9 behind the second; Jas 1:27 behind the third; 2Ti 2:24-25 behind the fourth.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a desideratum as that which is not possessed, but which is desirable; and reform, as to change from worse to better; to amend.
webster_full: DESIDERA'TUM, n. That which is not possessed, but which is desirable; any perfection or improvement which is wanted.
REFORM', v.t. To change from worse to better; to amend; to correct; to restore to a former good state.
EDIFY, v.t. To instruct and improve the mind in knowledge generally, and particularly in moral and religious knowledge, faith and holiness.
scriptures: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
corruption_summary: Six proposals, all defensible from Scripture, which between them reshaped Protestantism for three centuries.
corruption_paragraphs: The document is worth reading because almost every later evangelical reform programme is a variation on it: Bible study groups, lay ministry, experiential preaching, irenic controversy, practical seminary training. Act 17:11 supports the first proposal directly, with the Bereans searching the Scriptures daily rather than waiting to be told. 2Ti 3:16 makes the whole Scripture profitable, which means profitable to the whole congregation.

The defect is in what the six leave unguarded. None of them states that the content of doctrine must be fixed and defended, and the fourth, taken alone, can be read as a counsel against controversy rather than a counsel about its manner. Spener himself did not intend that, but his successors increasingly did, and Pietism's later history in Germany runs from warm orthodoxy toward a religion of feeling that could not resist rationalism when it came. The principle to recover is that reform of practice must be chained to confession of doctrine.
roots_lines: Greek anakrino (G350) — to search, to examine; Acts 17:11.
usage: “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable” (2Ti 3:16) — proposal one.
“a royal priesthood” (1Pe 2:9) — proposal two.
“searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11) — the practice proposed for every household.

pos: n. (August Hermann Francke, 1663–1727, professor at Halle, founder of the Halle orphanage and institutions)
etymology: Latin Augustus, venerable; German Francke, a Frank, a free man.
biblical_def: August Hermann Francke was converted at Lüneburg in 1687 while preparing a sermon on John 20:31, expelled from Leipzig and then Erfurt for his Pietist meetings, and in 1692 appointed professor of Greek and oriental languages at the new university of Halle and pastor of nearby Glaucha. Finding the parish wretched, he put a box on his wall for alms, and from what went into it built a school for the poor, then an orphanage, then a Latin school, a teachers' seminary, a dispensary, a publishing house and a Bible institute that printed cheap Scriptures by the hundred thousand — the Halle Institutions, housing thousands, funded by prayer and gifts without endowment. Halle trained the first Protestant missionaries to India and supplied the Church Missionary Society's first men. Jas 1:27 is the institution's charter, visiting the fatherless in their affliction. Mat 9:38 is the prayer Halle answered for a century.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an orphan as a child who is bereaved of father or mother, or of both; and charity, as liberality to the poor.
webster_full: OR'PHAN, n. A child who is bereaved of father or mother, or of both.
CHAR'ITY, n. In a general sense, love, benevolence, good will. Liberality to the poor, consisting in almsgiving or benefactions.
INSTITU'TION, n. The act of establishing; establishment; a system or body of principles; a society established for some object.
scriptures: Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Mat 9:38
Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.
Mat 5:16
Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.
The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that winneth souls is wise.
corruption_summary: An alms box on a parish wall grew into schools, an orphanage, a press and the first Protestant mission to India.
corruption_paragraphs: Francke's method was to begin with what was in front of him and refuse to stop. He did not plan the Halle Institutions; he taught poor children, then housed orphans, then needed teachers, then needed books, then needed a press, then found men who wanted to carry the books abroad. Jas 1:27 names the starting point, and the rest followed because he treated each new need as the next instance of the same command.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live question is one of funding and faith. Francke published annual accounts of the Institutions showing gifts arriving as needs arose, and the practice of unendowed, prayer-funded charity passed from him to Zinzendorf, to Whitefield's Georgia orphanage and to Müller at Bristol. Mat 5:16 is the point of the publicity: the works are seen so that the Father is glorified, which is why Francke printed the accounts.
roots_lines: Greek episkeptomai (G1980) — to visit, to look after; James 1:27.
usage: “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jas 1:27) — the alms box.
“that he will send forth labourers into his harvest” (Mat 9:38) — and Halle sent them.
“that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father” (Mat 5:16) — why he printed the accounts.

pos: n. (Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg, 1682–1719, Halle Pietist, first Protestant missionary to India, at Tranquebar from 1706)
etymology: Greek Bartholomaios, son of Talmai; German Ziegenbalg, goatskin.
biblical_def: Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg was a Halle student sent with Heinrich Plütschau by Frederick IV of Denmark to the Danish settlement at Tranquebar on the Coromandel coast, landing in July 1706 as the first Protestant missionaries to India. The Danish authorities on the spot opposed them and imprisoned Ziegenbalg for four months. He learned Tamil by sitting on the floor of a school with the children, compiled a Tamil grammar and dictionary, translated the New Testament into Tamil by 1711 and most of the Old before his death at thirty-six, set up a press, founded schools for boys and for girls, and wrote careful studies of South Indian religion based on reading its own texts — work Halle suppressed as unnecessary. He insisted the church be Tamil, with Tamil preachers and Tamil hymns. Isa 55:11 is the promise behind the translation. Rev 7:9 the end he worked toward. Act 17:11 the practice he taught his converts.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a missionary as one sent to propagate religion; and vernacular, as native; belonging to the country of one's birth.
webster_full: MIS'SIONARY, n. One sent to propagate religion.
VERNAC'ULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth. We say, the vernacular tongue.
GRAM'MAR, n. The art of speaking or writing a language with propriety, according to established usage.
scriptures: So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
Rev 7:9

After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands;
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
corruption_summary: He sat on a schoolroom floor with Tamil children until he could translate the New Testament, and died at thirty-six.
corruption_paragraphs: Ziegenbalg settled, in 1706, questions the missionary movement kept relitigating for two centuries. Should the Scriptures be put into the vernacular as a first priority? He did it within five years of landing. Should converts be formed into a church with their own ministers and their own hymns, or kept as dependents? He trained Tamil catechists from the start. Should a missionary study the religion he is addressing? He read the Tamil texts and wrote two books on them, which his own sponsors declined to print, judging that the business was to uproot error and not describe it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Halle's refusal to publish his studies was the error, and the correction is Act 17, where Paul reads Athens before he preaches to it. Act 17:11 then shows what the converts do with the text once they have it. Rev 7:9 is the warrant for a church that is Tamil and not German: the multitude before the throne is of all kindreds and tongues, and the tongues are not erased on the way in.
roots_summary: Hebrew dabar (H1697), word; Greek glossa (G1100), tongue; anakrino (G350), to examine.
roots_lines: Greek glossa (G1100) — a tongue, a language; Revelation 7:9.
Greek phule (G5443) — a kindred, a tribe; Revelation 7:9.
usage: “it shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11) — the Tamil New Testament of 1711.
“of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” (Rev 7:9) — a Tamil church.
“searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11) — what he gave his converts the means to do.

pos: n. (Tranquebar, Danish Tranquebar or Tharangambadi, a Danish trading settlement on the Coromandel coast of India, 1620–1845)
etymology: Tamil Tharangambadi, the place of the singing waves; Danish Trankebar.
biblical_def: Tranquebar was a fortified Danish factory of a few square miles on the Tamil coast, leased from the Nayak of Thanjavur in 1620, and it became the cradle of Protestant missions in Asia. Frederick IV of Denmark, pressed by his Halle-trained court chaplain, sent Ziegenbalg and Plütschau there in 1706 because it was the only Indian ground under a Protestant crown. The Danish-Halle Mission that grew from it produced the Tamil Bible, the first Protestant press in India, schools, and a line of missionaries running through Schwartz into the nineteenth century. The settlement itself was commercially insignificant and the local Danish officials were mostly hostile to the mission, imprisoning Ziegenbalg and obstructing his successors. Its importance was entirely accidental to its purpose, which is a pattern worth noticing. Zec 4:6 is the comment. Act 16:9 is how such doors open. Mat 28:19 is what came through it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a factory as a house or place where factors reside, to transact business for their employers; and a settlement, as the act of settling, or state of being settled; a colony.
webster_full: FAC'TORY, n. A house or place where factors reside, to transact business for their employers.
SET'TLEMENT, n. The act of settling, or state of being settled; a colony recently established.
COL'ONY, n. A company of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country.
scriptures: Zec 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
Act 16:9
And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us.
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
corruption_summary: A failing Danish trading post of a few square miles became the door through which Protestant missions entered Asia.
corruption_paragraphs: The lesson of Tranquebar is about how God uses what men build for other purposes. The Danes did not plant the settlement to carry the gospel and their officers there resisted it. The king's interest came from a chaplain. The missionaries were German, not Danish, because no Dane volunteered. Zec 4:6 fits the whole sequence: not by might, nor by power.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The caution worth stating is that colonial infrastructure was a real instrument and a real liability for missions, opening doors and then tying the gospel in local eyes to foreign power. Ziegenbalg saw it and built a Tamil church with Tamil ministers in response. Act 16:9 describes a door opened by vision rather than by commerce, and the two kinds of door are not equally safe. Mat 28:19 is the commission either way.
roots_summary: Hebrew chayil (H2428), might; Greek horama (G3705), a vision; ethnos (G1484), nation.
usage: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit” (Zec 4:6) — a few square miles of beach.
“Come over into Macedonia, and help us” (Act 16:9) — how the better doors open.
“Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Mat 28:19) — what came through this one.

pos: n. (Christian Friedrich Schwartz, 1726–1798, Danish-Halle missionary in South India for forty-eight years)
etymology: Greek Christianos, a follower of Christ; German Schwartz, black.
biblical_def: Christian Friedrich Schwartz went to Tranquebar in 1750 as a Halle man and never came home. He served forty-eight years in Tranquebar, Tiruchirappalli and Thanjavur, learning Tamil, Persian, Hindustani and English, preaching in whichever the occasion required, living with almost no possessions. His integrity became proverbial to the point of embarrassment: when the East India Company and the Nawab of Arcot could not trust each other's envoys, Haidar Ali of Mysore said he would deal with the Christian, and Schwartz was sent on an embassy he had no wish to make. The Raja of Thanjavur made him guardian of his adopted heir. He built schools, founded congregations, and trained Indian catechists. He kept clear of politics except where asked and refused payment for it. 2Co 5:20 names the office he actually held, ambassador for Christ. Mat 5:16 names what the courts saw. Pro 11:30 names the object he never lost sight of.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines integrity as the entire, unimpaired state of any thing; probity; honesty; and an ambassador, as a minister of the highest rank, employed by one prince at the court of another.
webster_full: INTEG'RITY, n. The entire, unimpaired state of any thing; particularly of the mind; moral soundness or purity; incorruptness; uprightness; honesty.
AMBAS'SADOR, n. A minister of the highest rank employed by one prince or state, at the court of another.
CAT'ECHIST, n. One who instructs by question and answer, particularly in the rudiments of the Christian religion.
scriptures: Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ's stead, be ye reconciled to God.
Mat 5:16
Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.
The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that winneth souls is wise.
Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
corruption_summary: A Hindu ruler who trusted no European diplomat said he would treat with the Christian, and meant it as a description.
corruption_paragraphs: The Haidar Ali episode is quoted so often that its edge is blunted. The point is not that a missionary was admired; it is that in a region where every European was assumed to be purchasable, one man's word was taken as security by a ruler at war with the people who sent him. Mat 5:16 is the mechanism: the works are seen, and the glory goes to the Father. Nothing Schwartz preached would have carried half the weight without them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The risk his career illustrates is real: a missionary used as a diplomat is a missionary entangled, and the Thanjavur regency drew him into administration for years. He kept the distinction by refusing fees and by never ceasing to preach. 2Co 5:20 defines the only embassy that finally mattered, praying men in Christ's stead to be reconciled to God, and Pro 11:30 the only success worth counting.
roots_summary: Greek presbeuo (G4243), to be an ambassador; katallasso (G2644), to reconcile; kalos (G2570), good.
roots_lines: Greek presbeuo (G4243) — to act as an ambassador; 2 Corinthians 5:20.
Hebrew laqach (H3947) — to take, to win; Proverbs 11:30.

“that they may see your good works” (Mat 5:16) — and Haidar Ali did.
“he that winneth souls is wise” (Pro 11:30) — the only count he kept.

pos: n. (Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf, 1700–1760, Saxon count, patron and bishop of the renewed Moravian Brethren)
etymology: Greek Nikolaos, conqueror of the people; Zinzendorf, an Austrian noble house.
biblical_def: Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf was Spener's godson, raised by a Pietist grandmother and educated at Francke's Halle, who as a young count gave refuge on his Berthelsdorf estate in 1722 to Moravian refugees, the remnant of the old Bohemian Brethren of Hus. The settlement they built was Herrnhut. He gave his fortune and his life to them, was made a bishop, was exiled from Saxony for eleven years, and organized a missionary enterprise out of a village of a few hundred that sent men to the West Indies, Greenland, Suriname, South Africa and Labrador within two decades. His theology centred relentlessly on the wounds and blood of Christ, in terms that in his middle years became extravagant to the point of embarrassment, and he later restrained them. Gal 6:14 is his genuine centre, glorying in nothing but the cross. 2Co 5:14 is the engine: “For the love of Christ constraineth us.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a count as a title of foreign nobility; and brethren, as the plural of brother, used in the solemn and scriptural style.
webster_full: COUNT, n. A title of foreign nobility, equivalent to the English earl.
BRETH'REN, n. plu. of brother. It is used almost exclusively in solemn and scriptural language, in the place of brothers.
DIAS'PORA usage follows DISPER'SION, n. The act of scattering; the state of being scattered.
scriptures: Gal 6:14
But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world.
For the love of Christ constraineth us; because we thus judge, that if one died for all, then were all dead:
Rev 7:9

After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands;
Act 1:8

But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.
corruption_summary: A village of a few hundred refugees sent missionaries to four continents in twenty years because a count spent his estate on them.
corruption_paragraphs: Zinzendorf's excesses should be stated plainly, because his admirers often skip them. In the Sifting Time of the 1740s the Herrnhut communities' devotion to the side-wound of Christ produced hymnody and imagery that was sentimental where it was not grotesque, and the count bore the responsibility and afterwards suppressed much of it. Gal 6:14 is the discipline the excess lacked: glorying in the cross, by which the world is crucified to the believer, is sober and outward-facing language.

What survived the correction is extraordinary. 2Co 5:14 explains the Moravian missionary economy better than any strategy document: men went to Saint Thomas and Greenland with no society, no salary and no prospect of return, supporting themselves by trade. Act 1:8 names the reach and Rev 7:9 the end. The principle to recover is that an intense Christ-centred piety, kept under the discipline of the text, produces senders and goers in numbers no committee can manufacture.
roots_summary: Greek stauros (G4716), a cross; sunecho (G4912), to constrain; ethnos (G1484), nation.
roots_lines: Greek kauchaomai (G2744) — to glory, to boast; Galatians 6:14.
Greek sunecho (G4912) — to constrain, to press; 2 Corinthians 5:14.
usage: “God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal 6:14) — his true centre.
“For the love of Christ constraineth us” (2Co 5:14) — the Moravian missionary economy.
“unto the uttermost part of the earth” (Act 1:8) — Greenland, Labrador, Saint Thomas.

pos: n. (Herrnhut, the Moravian settlement founded 1722 on Count Zinzendorf's Berthelsdorf estate in Upper Lusatia, Saxony)
etymology: German Herrn Hut, the Lord's watch or the Lord's protection.
biblical_def: Herrnhut means the Lord's watch, and the village earned the name twice. Founded in 1722 by Moravian refugees under Christian David, it grew within five years into a quarrelsome settlement of several hundred from a dozen backgrounds, near to breaking apart. Zinzendorf drew up a Brotherly Agreement in May 1727, and on 13 August, at a communion service in the Berthelsdorf church, the community experienced a reconciliation its members regarded for the rest of their lives as the day the Spirit came upon them. Out of it came the Stundengebet, a round-the-clock prayer watch in which members took hourly turns, which the Moravians maintained for over a hundred years, and out of that came the missionary enterprise of 1732 onward. Act 2:42 and Act 1 lie behind both the prayer and the sending. Mat 9:38 is the prayer itself: “Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a vigil as a watch; devotional watching; and intercession, as prayer or solicitation to one party in favor of another.
webster_full: VIG'IL, n. Watch; devotion performed in the customary hours of rest or sleep.
INTERCES'SION, n. The act of interceding; mediation; interposition between parties at variance, with a view to reconcilation; prayer or solicitation to one party in favor of another.
UNANIM'ITY, n. Agreement of a number of persons in opinion or determination; agreement in will.
scriptures: Mat 9:38
Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
Jas 5:16
Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.
Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
corruption_summary: A hundred-year prayer meeting, in hourly shifts, out of a village that had nearly torn itself apart five years earlier.
corruption_paragraphs: The sequence at Herrnhut is worth keeping in order, because it is usually told backwards. The famous unity of August 1727 did not fall on a harmonious community; it came after five years of faction and after a written agreement that bound the members to specific mutual duties. Jas 5:16 joins confessing faults one to another with praying one for another in a single verse, and that is precisely what the Brotherly Agreement and the watch did, in that order.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The temptation is to want the prayer watch without the reconciliation, or the reconciliation without the written agreement that made it concrete. Ecc 4:9 is unglamorous and exactly right: two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labour. Mat 9:38 is what they prayed for an hundred years, and Act 2:42 the four-fold shape that kept the praying inside a church.
roots_summary: Greek deomai (G1189), to pray; ergates (G2040), labourer; proskartereo (G4342), to continue stedfastly.
roots_lines: Greek deomai (G1189) — to beseech, to pray; Matthew 9:38.
usage: “Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest” (Mat 9:38) — hourly, for a hundred years.
“Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another” (Jas 5:16) — in that order, in 1727.
“Two are better than one” (Ecc 4:9) — the Brotherly Agreement in a sentence.

pos: n. (Christian David, 1692–1751, Moravian carpenter, founder of Herrnhut and missionary to Greenland)
etymology: Greek Christianos, a follower of Christ; Hebrew David, beloved.
biblical_def: Christian David was a Moravian carpenter, raised Roman Catholic, who was converted while working as a journeyman in Görlitz and spent the rest of his life walking. He led the first families of Moravian refugees out of Moravia in 1722 and felled the first tree at Herrnhut with his own axe; he made some ten journeys back into Moravia to bring others out, at the risk of imprisonment, and perhaps three hundred came. He served as the settlement's builder and lay preacher, went to Greenland in 1733 and built the mission house at New Herrnhut, worked in Suriname and among the Moravians in Pennsylvania, and kept returning to Herrnhut to take up his tools. John Wesley, who met him at Herrnhut in 1738, recorded his conversations with care. 1Co 15:58 is the word over such a life. Psa 127:1 is what he would have said about the houses he built.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a carpenter as an artificer who works in timber; a framer and builder of houses; and a refugee, as one who flees for refuge to another country.
webster_full: C'ARPENTER, n. An artificer who works in timber; a framer and builder of houses, and of ships.
REFUGEE', n. One who flies to a shelter or place of safety; one who, in times of persecution or political commotion, flees to a foreign country for safety.
ARTIF'ICER, n. An artist; a mechanic or manufacturer; one whose occupation requires skill or knowledge of a particular kind.
scriptures: Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
corruption_summary: He felled the first tree at Herrnhut and went back into Moravia ten times to bring out more people.
corruption_paragraphs: Christian David is the lay workman at the centre of a story usually told about a count. He had no education, preached in a plain style the Halle men found rough, and built with his hands the settlements the Moravians prayed in. Psa 127:1 was his trade and his doctrine in one verse: except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it, which a carpenter has particular reason to believe.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the man who clears the ground is not support staff for the ministry; he is in it. Act 8:4 has the scattered preaching everywhere they went, and the scattered were ordinary believers, not apostles. Heb 11:38 covers the ten journeys back into Moravia, and 1Co 15:58 promises that none of the building was wasted.
roots_summary: Greek kopos (G2873), labour; Hebrew banah (H1129), to build; Greek diaspeiro (G1289), to scatter.
usage: “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58) — said of a carpenter's work.
“Except the LORD build the house” (Psa 127:1) — his trade and his doctrine.
“went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4) — ten journeys back into Moravia.

pos: n. (Hans Egede, 1686–1758, Norwegian Lutheran pastor, missionary to Greenland from 1721, called the apostle of Greenland)
etymology: Danish-Norwegian Hans, a form of Johannes; Egede, from a Norwegian farm name.
biblical_def: Hans Egede was a Lutheran pastor in the Lofoten islands who became convinced that the Norse colonies planted in Greenland in the tenth century must still exist, cut off from the church for three hundred years, and spent a decade petitioning Copenhagen to let him go to them. He sailed in 1721 with his wife Gertrud and their children. There were no Norse; they had died out. He stayed anyway, among the Inuit, for fifteen years, learning Kalaallisut, translating, and enduring a failed trading company, scurvy and hostility. In 1733 a smallpox epidemic brought by a returning Greenlander killed perhaps two thirds of the population of the district; Egede and his family nursed the dying, and Gertrud died of exhaustion in 1735. He took her body home the next year and spent his last years training missionaries for the work. Mat 9:37 is the field he found. 1Co 15:58 is what held him when the errand failed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an apostle, secondarily, as the first preacher of the gospel in a country; and pestilence, as plague; any contagious disease that is epidemic and mortal.
webster_full: APOS'TLE, n. The word is also applied to the first preacher of the gospel in any country.
PES'TILENCE, n. Plague, appropriately so called; but in a general sense, any contagious or infectious disease that is epidemic and mortal.
CAT'ECHIST, n. One who instructs by question and answer in the rudiments of the Christian religion.
scriptures: Mat 9:37
Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;
Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.
corruption_summary: He went to Greenland to find a lost Norse church, found none, and stayed fifteen years among the people who were there.
corruption_paragraphs: Egede's premise was wrong and his obedience was not. A man who has spent ten years arguing for a mission and arrives to find its object does not exist has every excuse to sail home. He read the situation instead as the field God had actually given him. Mat 9:37 says the harvest is plenteous and the labourers few, and the verse does not add that the harvest must be the one the labourer expected.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The smallpox epidemic is the part that must not be softened. The disease came with European contact, the Egedes were part of that contact, and the mission's most Christlike hour — nursing the dying through a winter until his wife died of it — was spent among people his own civilization had infected. Jas 1:27 defines pure religion as visiting the afflicted, and that winter is what the definition looks like. Psa 126:6 promises the weeping sower his sheaves.
roots_summary: Greek therismos (G2326), harvest; kopos (G2873), labour; Hebrew bakah (H1058), to weep.
usage: “The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37) — not the harvest he expected.
“To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jas 1:27) — the smallpox winter.
“He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed” (Psa 126:6) — fifteen years of it.
